Product of Simple Fractions

FractionsAreaArithmetic
Game: See why multiplying two fractions means multiplying the tops and multiplying the bottoms.
How to play: Change the two fractions on the left and right. The middle square puts them together and shows the answer in red.

Look for the math

Why is p/q × r/s = pr/qs? The rule can look like a trick to memorise, but the picture makes it a matter of counting cells.

A fraction is parts of a whole

The fraction p/q, read "p q-ths", means p parts out of q equal ones. The left square is cut into q rows and p of them are green. The right square shows r/s the other way: s columns, r of them blue.

Cutting the parts smaller

Lay the rows over the columns. Every column is now cut into q cells, so r/s = rq/sq: r parts out of s are the same as rq parts out of sq. These are equivalent fractions. Taking p/q of that means keeping p rows out of every q: in each blue column that is p cells, pr cells in all, out of the qs cells of the square. Those are the cells inside the red outline, coloured both ways.

p/q × r/s = pr/qs

The test counted the cells for every pair of fractions with denominators up to 20, 44,100 pairs.

Simplifying

The product the picture gives, pr/qs, may not be in lowest terms: 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2. "Simplify fractions" divides each fraction by the greatest common divisor of its two numbers; the value never changes. In the applet the button stayed on once pressed and went on simplifying every fraction you made; here it simplifies once.

Make both fractions 1/2. How much of the square is coloured both ways? Now try 2/4 and 3/6: the picture changes, the answer does not.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
